newsitem.title: UK: German oil sale plan could hit world prices.
newsitem.headline: German oil sale plan could hit world prices.

text.p: Germany's plan to sell about 20 percent of its strategic oil reserves to help plug holes in government finances left oil markets unruffled on Thursday but analysts said an early sale could push international crude prices lower.

The Economics Ministry in Bonn said it was thinking of selling 7.3 million tonnes of crude oil in stages and would decide whether to proceed by July 11 when the cabinet is due to approve a supplementary budget.

Under the German plan, proposed by junior coalition partner the Free Democrats, the entire federal government crude reserve of 7.3 million tonnes, stored in salt caverns near the northern port town of Wilhelmshaven since 1975, would be sold.
World benchmark Brent Blend crude on London's International Petroleum Exchange was valued at $17.50 a barrel on Thursday, having lost $3 since mid-May.
Industry sources said if German sales started during the summer months when oil demand is usually slack, prices could resume their downward path.

"If they did it in the middle of a cold winter then it would probably moderate prices but if the oil came onto the market today it would have a much stronger impact," said Peter Bogin at Cambridge Energy Research Associates (CERA) in Paris.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt was quoted by the Handelsblatt business newspaper as saying the sales could raise about 500 million marks a year in both 1997 and 1998. He said there would be no impact on world oil markets.
The sale of 7.3 million tonnes of crude oil over the remainder of this year and 1998 would add some 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) to world supplies, the equivalent of a large new North Sea oilfield.

"It may be expedient for budgetary requirements but even though it's only 100,000 bpd, it's another nail in a bearish coffin," said Russell Hill, senior crude trader in London for Austrian oil company OMV.

The collapse of government plans to reap billions of marks in profits from a revaluation of Bundesbank gold reserves has left Bonn searching for alternative ways to cut its budget deficit this year and next to meet strict borrowing requirements for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Germany has very few hydrocarbon reserves of its own and is Europe's biggest oil importer.
Last year, it imported about 2.1 million bpd of crude oil and between 600,000 and 700,000 bpd of refined products like gasoline and heating oil.

Western countries built up strategic oil reserves, under the auspices of the International Energy Agency (IEA), following the 1970s Arab oil embargo to try and shield themselves from oil price shocks and supply disruption.

The bulk of the country's strategic reserves of around 100 days of supply are held by a Hamburg-based agency EBV on behalf of German oil companies. European Union and OECD commitments require Germany to maintain stocks of 90 days of supplies of major oil products.
EBV reserves can only be released back to the refineries by government order in times of international crisis.
Analysts said the proposal also reflected a more relaxed attitude about supply security at a senior level in Europe's most oil import-dependent economy.
"What is striking is that a country like Germany without any oil of its own feels comfortable enough to get rid of 20-days worth of stock cover," said CERA's Bogin.
German refineries would be at the front of any queue to buy the federal stocks but some could find its way onto the international spot market.
"Of course if the (government) makes an interesting offer we would be interested but it would depend on the price and the condition (of the crude)," said a senior trader for a leading German refiner.
